37958:
Rome had a large Jewish community, perhaps tens of thousands strong, spread across several synagogues in the districts across the Tiber. The message about Jesus probably arrived there through Jewish travellers and pilgrims (Acts 2:10 mentions visitors from Rome at Pentecost), so the first Roman believers met within or alongside the synagogues. Nobody knows who founded the church; Paul says he did not, and no early source credibly names Peter as founder at this date.

The Roman historian Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because they were constantly rioting 'at the instigation of Chrestus' (Claudius 25.4). Many historians think 'Chrestus' is a garbled form of 'Christus', meaning arguments in the synagogues about Jesus the Messiah. Acts confirms that Priscilla and Aquila had to leave Rome under Claudius (Acts 18:2). If Jewish believers were away for some years, the house churches would have become largely Gentile in leadership and habits. When the Jewish believers came back after 54, they found churches that ate differently and kept different days. This reconstruction (popularised by Wolfgang Wiefel and Peter Lampe) is widely used but not certain; it explains Romans 14-15 and Paul's warning to Gentiles not to look down on Israel (Rom 11:17-21) well.

Paul writes at a turning point. He considers his work in the eastern Mediterranean done (Rom 15:19-23). He is about to deliver money from Gentile churches to the poor believers in Jerusalem, a gift he sees as proof that Jews and Gentiles are one family (Rom 15:26-27), and he fears both unbelievers in Judea and the Jerusalem church's reception (Rom 15:31). Then he wants to go west to Spain, a land with few Jews and no synagogues to start from. Romans is therefore part theology, part peace-making, and part mission support letter: Paul lays out what he preaches so that a church which has heard rumours about him (Rom 3:8) can trust him and stand with him.
37960: There were no church buildings. Believers met in homes or in the back rooms of workshops, perhaps 20 to 40 people each. Romans greets 'the church in their house' of Priscilla and Aquila and other groups named by household (Rom 16:5, Rom 16:10-11, Rom 16:14-15). Different houses could easily develop different practices, which is part of why Paul pleads for welcome.
37962: Phoebe is called a diakonos (servant or minister) of the church at Cenchreae and a prostatis, a word used for a patron or benefactor who uses wealth and status to support others. Letters were carried and often read aloud and explained by the courier, so Phoebe was probably the first person to perform and interpret Romans in Rome.
37963: In a society that ranked people by honour, a crucified Messiah was shameful. Paul's 'I am not ashamed of the gospel' is a public claim to honour in a message the world despised. He also reverses status games: no one can boast before God, Jew or Greek (Rom 3:27), and believers are to outdo one another in showing honour (Rom 12:10).
37965: Jews kept kosher food laws and the Sabbath as signs of belonging to God's covenant. Some believers (Paul calls them 'weak in faith') ate only vegetables, probably to avoid meat that was not kosher or had been offered to idols, and kept special days. Others ate anything. Paul agrees in principle with the 'strong' but tells them not to wreck a brother's faith over dinner.
37967: Roman adoption gave an outsider, often an adult, the full name, rights and inheritance of a new father, and cancelled old debts. Paul uses it both for Gentiles brought into God's family and for Israel's own calling as God's son.
37969: Roman believers lived in the capital of an empire that called Caesar lord and saviour. Paul's teaching on governing authorities comes right after commands not to take revenge, and the empire's sword was a daily reality for a small, suspected minority.
37970:
Romans is a Jewish letter about the faithfulness of Israel's God. Its first sentence calls the gospel something God 'promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures' about a son of David (Rom 1:2-3), and it quotes the Jewish Scriptures more than any other letter of Paul, over fifty times. The key phrase 'the righteousness of God' (Rom 1:17, Rom 3:21) would remind a Jewish hearer of the Psalms and Isaiah, where God's righteousness is his covenant faithfulness: his commitment to put things right and rescue his people (Ps 98:2-3, Isa 46:13). So the question underneath the letter is not only 'how can I be saved?' but 'has God been faithful to what he promised Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through his family?' (Rom 4:16-18).

That is why chapters 9-11 are not a detour. If most of Israel has not accepted Jesus as Messiah, has God's word failed (Rom 9:6)? Paul, writing with grief for his own people (Rom 9:2-3), answers no: Israel's 'stumbling' is temporary and serves the inclusion of the nations, Gentiles are wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree, not a replacement tree, and 'all Israel will be saved' (Rom 11:17-26). The gifts and calling of God are irrevocable (Rom 11:29).

Scholars read this Jewishness in different ways. Traditional Reformed and Lutheran readers (Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner) see Paul showing that Jews too need to be justified by faith, not by doing the Law. The New Perspective (E. P. Sanders, James Dunn, N. T. Wright) stresses that first-century Judaism was a religion of grace and covenant, and that Paul's target is the use of Torah as a badge that keeps Gentiles out. The 'Paul within Judaism' school (Mark Nanos, Pamela Eisenbaum, Paula Fredriksen) goes further: Paul remained a Torah-observant Jew, and his letters address Gentiles about how they, as Gentiles, join Israel's God without becoming Jews. All three agree that Romans makes no sense unless it is read as a Jew's argument about Israel's Scriptures, Israel's Messiah and the destiny of Israel and the nations together.
37971: Paul introduces himself and the good news about the Davidic Messiah, now powerful to save the Jew first and also the Greek.
37973: Gentile idolatry and Jewish failure alike show that all humanity stands guilty before God; having the Law does not exempt anyone.
37975: God has acted in Jesus' sacrificial death to put right all who trust, as Abraham trusted before circumcision.
37977: Believers are at peace with God, freed from sin's reign, and joined to the risen Christ in baptism.
37979: The good Law could not overcome sin in the flesh, but the Spirit gives life, adoption and an unbreakable hope.
37981: Paul wrestles with Israel's unbelief and insists God has not rejected his people; all Israel will be saved.
37983: Mercy creates a new way of life: renewed minds, mutual love, non-retaliation and respect for authorities.
37985: Strong and weak, Jew and Gentile, must welcome each other as Christ welcomed them, so the church can support the mission to Spain.
37986: God's faithful righteousness in the Messiah
38013: Being in the right, and God's own faithfulness in putting things right. To 'justify' is to declare someone in the right, like a verdict in court, but in Romans it also means being counted part of God's covenant family. Traditional readers stress the legal verdict; New Perspective readers stress covenant membership; many hold both.
38015: Trust, but also loyalty and reliability. 'The faith of Jesus Christ' (Rom 3:22) can mean faith in Christ or Christ's own faithfulness; scholars are divided. Paul pairs it with obedience in 'the obedience of faith' (Rom 1:5).
38017: A gift from a benefactor. In ancient culture a gift created a relationship and expected gratitude. Paul's shock is that God gives to the unworthy, even enemies (Rom 5:6-10), which John Barclay calls the 'incongruity' of grace.
38019: The same word the Greek Old Testament uses for the lid of the ark of the covenant where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement. Translators debate whether 'propitiation' (turning away wrath) or 'expiation' (removing sin) is closer; many now render it 'mercy seat' or 'place of atonement'.
38021: Usually the Torah given to Israel at Sinai. Paul calls it holy, just and good (Rom 7:12), yet says it could not give life because of sin. Sometimes nomos means 'principle' or 'rule' (Rom 7:21-23).
38023: Being made a son and heir. Paul applies it to believers by the Spirit and lists it first among Israel's privileges.
38024: Abraham is Paul's main test case: he was counted righteous by trusting God's promise before he was circumcised, so he is father of both Jewish and Gentile believers.
38025: Paul's theme verse quotes Habakkuk's 'the righteous will live by faith(fulness)', written when Babylon threatened Judah and God's people had to trust him through crisis.
38026: Isaiah supplies Paul's mission texts (beautiful feet of messengers), his remnant theology and his hope that a deliverer will come from Zion.
38027: Paul reads Moses' words about the word being near, in your mouth and heart, as pointing to the message of faith in Christ.
38028: Galatians is the heated first draft of themes Romans sets out calmly: Abraham, faith, Law, Spirit and the unity of Jew and Gentile.
38029: Acts tells of the collection trip Romans anticipates, Paul's arrest in Jerusalem, and how he finally reached Rome, as a prisoner rather than a missionary passing through.
38030: Jesus is presented as the Jewish Messiah, 'descended from David according to the flesh' and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection (Rom 1:3-4). He is the 'end' or 'goal' (telos) of the Law (Rom 10:4), the new Adam whose obedience undoes Adam's disobedience (Rom 5:18-19), and the servant of the circumcised who confirms the promises to the patriarchs so that Gentiles might glorify God (Rom 15:8-9). Christian readers have traditionally seen in Romans 3:25 the clearest statement of Christ's death as atoning sacrifice. Jewish readers, such as contributors to the Jewish Annotated New Testament, note that Paul's argument depends at every step on Israel's Scriptures and that Romans 11 refuses to write Israel out of God's future, which makes Romans an important text for Jewish-Christian dialogue.
38031: Romans as a timeless manual of individual salvation, with chapters 9-11 as a detour
38032: Romans is the Bible's systematic explanation of how a person gets saved: everyone has sinned (3:23), the wages of sin is death (6:23), Christ died for us (5:8), and whoever confesses and believes is saved (10:9-10). This 'Romans Road' is the heart of the letter. Chapters 9-11 deal with a separate topic, predestination or Israel, and chapters 12-16 are practical application.
38033: Krister Stendahl argued in 1963 and 1976 that the introspective Western conscience, shaped by Augustine and Luther, read its own guilt-questions into Paul, while Paul's real question was how Gentiles become part of God's people. N. T. Wright, James Dunn and Richard Hays add that chapters 9-11 are the climax: the whole letter asks whether God has been faithful to Israel and to his promise that Abraham's family would bless the nations. Chapters 14-15 show the practical aim: a Jewish-Gentile church eating together. Picking verses from across the letter to make a four-step tract is useful for evangelism but cuts the steps out of Paul's actual argument.
38034: Douglas Moo, Thomas Schreiner and Simon Gathercole agree that Romans is about Jews and Gentiles and that 9-11 are integral. But they argue that Paul's answer to the Jew-Gentile question is precisely that every individual, Jew or Gentile, is a sinner who must be justified by faith apart from works (Rom 3:20-24, Rom 4:4-5). The 'Romans Road' does accurately summarise real Pauline teaching, and Romans 1-8 does address the universal human plight. Both sides agree the letter is bigger than a tract, and that personal salvation and the formation of one people belong together.
38035: If Romans is only about my individual salvation, the church's unity across ethnic lines becomes optional. If it is only about ethnic unity, the personal call to repent and trust Christ fades. Paul holds both.
38036: Romans 9: individual predestination or Israel's calling?
38037: Romans 9 teaches that God chooses before birth which individuals will be saved and which will be lost, like Jacob and Esau, and that humans have no right to question this (Rom 9:13, Rom 9:20-21).
38038: Many interpreters, including James Dunn, N. T. Wright and Brian Abasciano, note that Paul is answering why most of Israel has not believed, and that his Old Testament examples (Jacob and Esau, Pharaoh, the potter in Jeremiah 18) are about nations and God's purposes in history. In Malachi, 'Jacob I loved, Esau I hated' refers to the peoples Israel and Edom. On this reading Romans 9 is about God's freedom to shape his covenant people and include Gentiles, and the chapter flows into 10-11, where Israel's hardening is partial and temporary and the door is open to all who call on the Lord (Rom 10:13).
38039: John Piper (The Justification of God, 1983), Thomas Schreiner and Douglas Moo answer that Paul's problem is precisely why some individual Israelites believe and others do not (Rom 9:6-8), so individual salvation is in view; that Paul's language of 'vessels of mercy' prepared for glory (Rom 9:23) is about eternal destiny; and that corporate election still involves individuals. This is a real scholarly disagreement, not a popular error, and it runs along the Calvinist-Arminian line. The popular mistake is to read Romans 9 alone, without Romans 10-11's ending in mercy for all (Rom 11:32).
38040: Both readings affect how Christians speak about Israel, assurance and God's character. Reading 9-11 as one unit protects against using Romans 9 to say God has finished with the Jewish people.
38041: Romans 13 as a blank cheque for any government
38042: Romans 13:1-7 means Christians must always obey the government because every authority is directly instituted by God; resisting the state is resisting God.
38043: The passage sits inside a section on love and not taking revenge (Rom 12:17-21, Rom 13:8-10). Paul is telling a small, vulnerable minority in the imperial capital, recently disrupted by the expulsion under Claudius and perhaps tempted to refuse taxes, not to give Rome a pretext for violence. Elsewhere Paul assumes rulers can crucify the Lord of glory (1 Cor 2:8), and Jewish tradition taught that God sets up kings yet judges them (Dan 2:21, Dan 4:17). Scholars such as Neil Elliott and Robert Jewett read the passage as pastoral caution, not a theory of the state.
38044: Evangelical commentators such as Moo and Schreiner reply that Paul does state a general principle: authority as such comes from God and is meant to restrain evil. But they agree it is not unconditional. Acts shows apostles obeying God rather than men when commanded to stop preaching (Acts 5:29), and the mainstream Reformed tradition, from Calvin's remarks on lesser magistrates onwards, allowed for limits. Both sides reject using Romans 13 to silence protest against injustice.
38045: This text was used to support both obedience to Nazi authorities and apartheid; reading it in context helps believers honour authority without giving it what belongs to God.
38046: Roman believers learned that their divisions over food and days were not small matters: Jew and Gentile eating together was a sign that God had kept his promise. They were asked to see Paul's mission as theirs and to send him on to Spain with their support.
38047: Romans still grounds Christian assurance (Rom 8:1, Rom 8:38-39) and shaped Augustine, Luther, Wesley and Barth. Read whole, it also asks churches divided by culture, class or politics to welcome each other, rejects Gentile arrogance toward the Jewish people, and ties personal faith to a shared mission.
38048: Paul tells a gifted, status-hungry church in a Roman boom town that the cross turns the world's ladder of honour upside down, and answers their questions about sex, food, worship and the resurrection in that light.
38050: Paul founded the church in Corinth around 50-51 and stayed about eighteen months (Acts 18:11). Sosthenes may be the synagogue leader beaten in front of Gallio's tribunal (Acts 18:17), later a believer, though the name was common.
38051: Paul names himself, refers to his founding visit and closes in his own hand (1 Cor 16:21). Clement of Rome, writing to Corinth around 96, refers back to this letter by name (1 Clement 47). Authorship is undisputed.
38052: Paul says he will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost (1 Cor 16:8) and sends greetings from the churches of Asia (1 Cor 16:19). He had already written an earlier letter that is now lost (1 Cor 5:9).
38053: The church Paul founded in Corinth: mostly Gentile converts, a few Jews, a handful of better-off householders and many ordinary workers and slaves
38054: Members of Chloe's household reported factions (1 Cor 1:11), and Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus brought a letter of questions (1 Cor 7:1, 1 Cor 16:17). The church was splitting along lines of favourite teachers, social rank and spiritual giftedness, while tolerating sexual sin and taking each other to court.
38055: Rome destroys the old Greek city of Corinth.
38056: Julius Caesar refounds Corinth as a Roman colony, Colonia Laus Iulia Corinthiensis, settled largely by freedmen.
38057: Gallio, brother of the philosopher Seneca, serves as proconsul of Achaia (dated by an inscription found at Delphi); Paul is brought before him (Acts 18:12-17).
38058: Isthmian Games are held near Corinth in alternate years (51 is one usually suggested while Paul was there), the background to Paul's runner and boxer images (1 Cor 9:24-27).
38059: Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus; Nero becomes emperor in October.
38060:
The Corinth Paul knew was a young city. The old Greek Corinth had been destroyed by Rome in 146 BC; Julius Caesar refounded it in 44 BC as a Roman colony, and many first settlers were freed slaves. By the 50s it was the capital of the province of Achaia and a booming trade hub on the narrow isthmus between two seas, with harbours at Lechaion and Cenchreae and a paved slipway (the diolkos) for dragging ships across. It was a place where people with money and ambition could climb quickly, and where public inscriptions advertised who had paid for what.

Archaeology shows that world. A paving stone near the theatre records that one Erastus laid the pavement at his own expense in return for being made aedile, a city official. Many scholars identify him with the 'Erastus the city treasurer' of Romans 16:23, written from Corinth; others, notably Steven Friesen, question the identification and the first-century dating, so it is suggestive rather than proven. The Delphi inscription that names Gallio as proconsul lets historians date Paul's first stay around 50-51, one of the firmest dates in Paul's life.

The church reflected the city. 'Not many of you were wise by human standards, not many powerful, not many of noble birth' (1 Cor 1:26) implies some were. Better-off members hosted the church and its meals, and the problems at the Lord's Supper, where some ate well while others went hungry (1 Cor 11:20-22), look like a Roman dinner party where guests were served according to rank. Members ranked teachers like celebrity orators (1 Cor 1:12, 1 Cor 3:4), went to civil courts where the wealthy usually won (1 Cor 6:1-8), and treated speaking in tongues as spiritual status. Paul's answer to all of it is the cross: God chose the shameful and weak to shame the wise and strong.
38062: As a Roman colony Corinth ran its affairs in Latin with Roman-style magistrates, and freedmen could gain wealth and office there that was barred to them in Rome. Honour was earned in public through benefactions and recorded in stone. Paul's boasting only in the Lord cuts against this.
38064: Greek cities prized polished public speakers (sophists) who charged fees and gathered fans. Paul deliberately refused to perform like them and worked with his hands instead of taking patronage (Acts 18:3), which some in Corinth saw as low-status.
38066: At Roman dinners the host's friends reclined in the dining room with the best food while lesser guests ate elsewhere and later. When the church copied this, the meal meant to show one body in Christ became a display of class. Paul says this is not the Lord's Supper at all.
38068: Most meat in the market had been offered to a god, and social life (guild meals, birthdays, civic feasts) happened in temple dining rooms; dining rooms have been excavated at Corinth's sanctuary of Asclepius. Refusing could cost a person business and friendships, which is why Paul gives a careful answer in three chapters.
38070: Accepting money from a patron put you under obligation to them. Paul's refusal to accept support in Corinth kept him free from the powerful but offended those who wanted him as their client-teacher, an issue that flares again in 2 Corinthians.
38072: In Roman society married women covered their heads in public as a sign of modesty, and men covering their heads was associated with leading pagan sacrifice. Paul's instructions are tangled up with these honour codes; how far they are cultural or permanent is debated.
38073:
Although written to mostly Gentile converts, 1 Corinthians assumes that these former idol-worshippers have been brought into Israel's story. Paul calls the wilderness generation 'our fathers' (1 Cor 10:1) to Gentile readers, which means Israel's ancestors are now theirs too. He retells the exodus, the manna, the water from the rock and the golden calf as warnings for them (1 Cor 10:1-11). He calls Christ 'our Passover lamb' and tells them to clean out the old leaven, as a Jewish household did before Passover (1 Cor 5:7-8), and he plans his travels around Pentecost (1 Cor 16:8).

The ethics are Jewish ethics. Paul's ban on sexual immorality and idolatry echoes what Jews required of Gentiles who turned to Israel's God (compare Acts 15:20), and his reasoning about the church as God's temple (1 Cor 3:16-17) imports the Jerusalem temple's holiness into a Gentile congregation. Most striking, Paul quotes the Shema, Israel's confession that the LORD is one (Deut 6:4), and expands it: 'one God, the Father... and one Lord, Jesus Christ' (1 Cor 8:6). Richard Bauckham and N. T. Wright see this as placing Jesus within the identity of Israel's one God, without abandoning Jewish monotheism.

Paula Fredriksen and other 'Paul within Judaism' scholars point out that Paul never tells these Gentiles to become Jews, but he does insist they stop worshipping other gods, which was the one thing pagan society found offensive. 'Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, but keeping the commandments of God' (1 Cor 7:19) shows a Jew who still thinks God's commands matter, while denying that Gentiles must become Jews. And the resurrection hope of chapter 15 is a Pharisaic, Jewish hope in the raising of bodies, not the Greek hope of a soul escaping its body.
38075: Factions boast in Paul, Apollos or Cephas; Paul answers with the foolish wisdom of a crucified Messiah.
38077: Incest, lawsuits and prostitution are incompatible with being a people bought with a price and indwelt by the Spirit.
38079: Answering their letter, Paul affirms marriage and sexual mutuality, and commends singleness for undivided devotion in a time of distress.
